reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Ashcraft Pediatric Surgery
clinicalPearls: A congenital hamartomatous lung lesion of cystic and/or solid tissue that communicates with the tracheobronchial tree
Increasingly detected on antenatal ultrasound as a cystic or echogenic lung mass, allowing planned postnatal assessment
Classified by cyst size into macrocystic and microcystic types, which influences prenatal behaviour and appearance
Large lesions can cause mediastinal shift, hydrops, and pulmonary hypoplasia in the fetus, while many involute or shrink relatively before birth
Postnatally it may be asymptomatic or cause respiratory distress, and later recurrent infection within the malformation
Cross-sectional CT after birth defines the anatomy and helps distinguish it from sequestration, which has a systemic arterial supply
Symptomatic lesions are resected, and elective resection of asymptomatic lesions is often advised because of infection and a small malignancy risk
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital pulmonary airway malformation arises from abnormal branching morphogenesis of the developing airways, producing a mass of disorganised, adenomatoid or cystic terminal respiratory structures that maintain communication with the bronchial tree but lack normal alveolar architecture. Depending on the level and timing of the developmental error, lesions vary from large single cysts to microcystic and solid tissue. Unlike bronchopulmonary sequestration, the blood supply is usually from the pulmonary circulation. Large lesions exert mass effect in utero, compressing normal lung and mediastinal structures, whereas after birth the abnormal, poorly draining airspaces predispose to air trapping and recurrent infection, and hybrid lesions with features of sequestration occur.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia with bowel in the chest
additionalInvestigations: Antenatal ultrasound with serial monitoring and CPAM volume assessment
Fetal MRI to characterise large or complex lesions and assess residual lung
Postnatal chest radiograph, though it may appear normal early
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to define anatomy and feeding vessels
Assessment for a systemic feeding artery to identify hybrid or sequestration components
Histological examination of the resected specimen to exclude malignancy
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory distress from a large space-occupying lesion
Fetal hydrops or significant mediastinal shift on prenatal imaging
Recurrent or severe infection within the malformation
Features suggesting pleuropulmonary blastoma rather than a benign lesion
Rapid enlargement or tension physiology causing cardiorespiratory compromise
reference.prognosis: Many small lesions are asymptomatic with an excellent outlook, and resection is generally curative with good long-term lung function. Large lesions causing fetal hydrops or severe pulmonary hypoplasia carry a worse prognosis, and the small associated malignancy risk supports specialist follow-up or elective resection.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal postnatal chest radiograph excludes a lesion seen antenatally
Failing to look for a systemic feeding vessel and misclassifying a hybrid lesion
Confusing a large cyst with congenital diaphragmatic hernia or lobar emphysema
Attributing recurrent pneumonia to ordinary infection and missing an underlying malformation
Overlooking the possibility of pleuropulmonary blastoma in an atypical cystic lesion
